steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Pins: cannot move, or should not move. This part covers What a pin costs; Ways out of a pin. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Cannot, or should not.** If the screened piece is the king, the pinned piece can move only along the line: an **absolute** pin. If it is anything else, moving is legal but costs what stands behind: a **relative** pin. Nimzowitsch spoke of whole and half pins: a piece that can slide along the line is only half pinned. The price is one comparison: what is behind, against what moves.

steps.prompt: Before you step on: can the black king capture or step onto d6? Say why in a few words.

fields.label: Can the king go to d6?

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f6 may legally move, but the line from g5 through f6 ends at the queen.

line.say: Suppose the knight retreats. The move is legal.
The bishop takes the queen, which the knight was shielding.
The king takes back. Black has given a queen for a bishop.

claims.statement: The knight on f6 has five legal moves.
After the knight leaves, the bishop attacks the queen.
Moving the knight loses a queen for a bishop along the engine line.

steps.text: **A pinned piece still bites.** It cannot leave the line, but it keeps attacking the squares it attacks, so the enemy king may not step onto them. A pinned knight is stuck completely, because a knight never moves along a line. Look at the board, then answer before you step on.

steps.title: Is the piece really pinned?
steps.prompt: Same kind of position, three small differences. For each, predict whether the attack on the bishop wins it.

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on e5 is pinned to its king by the rook on e8, but it still guards d6 and c7.

claims.statement: The king on d7 cannot step to d6 or c7, because the pinned bishop still controls them.
The rook on e8 attacks the bishop.

steps.caption: White to move. The same pin, but the rook behind the bishop is defended and is worth as much as White's rook.

line.say: The pawn attacks the pinned bishop.
The bishop leaves anyway. The rook behind it is defended, so taking it wins nothing.
White takes the rook with check.
The knight takes back. The rooks are swapped and nobody is ahead: a pin on a defended equal piece costs nothing.

claims.statement: The pawn push wins nothing along the engine line.
The engine rates the position as level.
The rook on e1 attacks the bishop.

steps.caption: White to move. The black knight on d5 is defended by the bishop on e6, which is pinned.

line.say: The knight takes. The bishop "defends" it but cannot recapture without exposing the king.
Black attacks the knight a second time, with the rook.
The knight steps back. White keeps the extra piece.

claims.statement: Capturing on d5 wins a piece along the engine line.
The bishop on e6 has no legal move.
The bishop is the only black piece that guards d5.

steps.text: **Why a pin bites.** A pinned piece cannot leave, so it can be attacked again and again. If it leaves, it pays. Nimzowitsch (*My System*, pin chapter) held that a pinned piece defends only on paper, and that a pawn is the best attacker, because it cannot be chased away. E. Lasker listed pins among the ways a defender is an illusion. [I] Cheaper attackers are usually better, but check the position.

steps.prompt: In the position where the attack failed, the bishop could simply move away. Which feature was different from the working position?

fields.label: What changed:
options: the king no longer stands behind the bishop
the white rook is not on the e-file
the pawn on f4 is missing
fields.answer: the king no longer stands behind the bishop

steps.caption: White to move. [I] One way a pin can end: White asks the bishop with a pawn, and the bishop trades itself for the knight, so White gets the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns. The engine prefers other moves at move 4 [V], so this is one way, not the only one.

line.say: Opens the f1 bishop. The knight on c3 stays pinned, so White builds around it.
Black castles. The bishop may stay on b4 as long as it likes.
Develops and keeps the c3 knight pinned, so Black must keep guarding d4.
Black stakes a claim in the centre and pressures c4.
The pawn forces the bishop to decide now, because a retreat gives up the pin for nothing.
Black gives up the bishop for the knight.
White has the bishop pair; the cost is the doubled c-pawns.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has no legal move at the start.
At the end White has doubled pawns on c3 and c4.

steps.text: **Five ways out of a pin.** The pinned side can **block** the line, **capture** the pinner, **step aside** (move the screened piece, or swap it for a cheaper one), **hit the pinner**, usually with a pawn, or **counter-attack** harder. [I] This sorting is mine. Nimzowitsch listed related policies: ask the pinner a question, ignore the pin, bring up reserves, or keep your options open. Check each answer before you lean on a pin.

steps.caption: Black to move. Way one: block the line. A bishop steps between the pinner and the king.

line.say: The bishop steps between the pinner and the king. The knight is free.
White takes the centre.
Black develops the other knight. The c6 knight is free to move whenever it wants.

claims.statement: The knight on c6 has no legal move at the start.
After the block the knight on c6 has five legal moves.

steps.caption: White to move. Way two: capture the pinner. The bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3, and the rook on b1 can take it.

line.say: The rook takes the pinner. The knight is free and White is a piece up.
Black has no way to take back.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has no legal move.
The rook attacks the bishop.
Capturing the pinner wins the bishop along the engine line.

steps.caption: White to move. Way three: step aside. The king leaves the diagonal, so the knight on d2 is no longer pinned.

line.say: The king steps off the diagonal. The pin is over and the knight may move, which it should, since the bishop still attacks it.

claims.statement: The knight on d2 has no legal move.
After the king steps aside the knight has six legal moves.

steps.caption: Black to move. Way three, second form: swap the piece behind. A bishop on e7 stands behind the knight and in front of the queen, so the pin now threatens only a defended bishop.

line.say: The bishop steps behind the knight, in front of the queen.
White can no longer win anything by capturing on f6, since the bishop recaptures.
The knight leaves. The white bishop now attacks only the bishop, which the queen and the king defend.

claims.statement: After the knight has left, the white bishop attacks the bishop on e7.
Two black pieces defend the bishop on e7.

steps.caption: White to move. Way four: hit the pinner. A pawn attack makes the bishop choose.

line.say: The pawn attacks the pinning bishop.
The bishop trades itself for the pinned knight, with check.
White recaptures and has both bishops, with doubled pawns on the c-file.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has no legal move.
After the pawn push, the pawn attacks the bishop.
After the trade only White owns both bishops.
After the recapture White has doubled pawns on c2 and c3.

steps.caption: [R] Way five: counter-attack. Optional extra. White to move. The old trap on this move has a name, the Elephant Trap. The pinned knight captures because the in-between check wins the queen back.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn on d5, hoping the pinned knight on f6 cannot recapture.
The pinned knight captures anyway. The queen is now exposed to the bishop.
White takes the queen.
Black checks first. The in-between move comes before any recapture.
White blocks the check with the queen.
The bishop takes the queen.
The king recaptures.
The king takes the bishop. Black has won a piece for a pawn.

claims.statement: The capture on d5 is worse than the best move by at least 300 centipawns.
Along the engine line the capture on d5 costs White a piece for a pawn.

steps.caption: [R] Optional extra: the pinned piece can bite back, because the bait is poisoned. White to move; the knight on f3 is pinned to the queen on d1.

line.say: The pinned knight moves anyway. Now the queen and the knight both attack the bishop on g4.
Black takes the knight.
The queen takes the bishop, and White ends a pawn ahead.

claims.statement: The knight capture is the engines first choice.
After the knight moves, the queen and the knight both attack the bishop.
White ends at least a pawn ahead along the engine line.

steps.caption: [R] If Black takes the queen instead, White has a finish. White to move.

line.say: The bishop gives check; the knight on e5 guards f7, so the king cannot take.
The king has only one square.
The knight gives checkmate.

claims.statement: White mates in two moves.

steps.text: **Remember.** A pinned piece has a more valuable piece behind it on the same line. If that piece is the king, it cannot move at all; otherwise it can move but costs what is behind. Ask what stands behind, and whether it is worth more. Defenders can block, capture the pinner, step aside, hit the pinner or counter-attack.
